bio.dissertation: Data-Driven Business Decision-Making with Causal Inference and Machine Learning

research_narrative:
Sikun studies how firms can make reliable decisions using modern machine
learning and AI systems when the available data is noisy, high-dimensional,
or hard to interpret directly. Her work sits at the intersection of three
threads: causal inference (so that the decisions firms make are driven by
what actually moves outcomes, not artifacts of selection or measurement),
machine learning on unstructured data (text, images, embeddings — the kind
of data that powers modern business systems but resists classical
econometric tools), and the statistical pitfalls of data-driven decision
pipelines themselves (where the act of choosing the best-looking policy
systematically biases what you think you've learned).

Her current papers develop methods for two specific versions of this
problem. The first builds a causal framework for using learned
representations of unstructured data as inputs to marketing and operations
decisions — moving beyond predictive accuracy to ask whether the
representations capture features that *cause* the outcome. The second
characterizes a "winner's curse" in data-driven decision-making: when
managers select among many candidate policies based on estimated
performance, the chosen winner is systematically overstated in expectation,
and she develops corrections that recover honest estimates.

Methodologically, Sikun draws on causal inference, deep learning, and
high-dimensional statistics. Substantively, she applies these tools to
quantitative marketing and quantitative finance.

about_md:
I am a Ph.D. candidate at Olin Business School, Washington University in St. Louis. I'm fortunate to be advised by Prof. [Dennis Zhang](http://denniszhang.org/) and Prof. [Raphael Thomadsen](https://sites.wustl.edu/thomadsen/). I study how firms can make reliable decisions using modern machine learning and AI systems when the available data is noisy and high-dimensional.
